Fold-change ratio

Microarray era...

  • Fold-change=Ratio
  • LogFC Fold-Change, LogRatio Sometimes
  • The fold change of X is used to detect DEGs

But

→\rightarrow Many false positive errors

A fold change on its own is the ratio of two noisy numbers. Without a test behind it, a large ratio is most often a small denominator.

Hypothesis testing

Five pictures of one idea: you never measure the truth, you measure a sample, and you decide what that sample is evidence for.

Testing for differential gene expression

  • Biological replicates are crucial
    • no replicates, no statistics, no p-value
  • The test is done as many times as there are genes
  • One needs to adjust the p-values for multiple hypothesis testing
No replicates, no variance. No variance, no p-value — only a ratio.

Two schools of probability

share of sixes after 10, 100, … 10,000 throws  ·  1/6

Neyman–Pearson · frequentist
A probability is a long-run frequency.

Throw it once and the word has nothing to attach to. You may only ask about what you could repeat.

→ P( data | hypothesis ) — the p-value

how sure I am of this die's chance of a six, after 10 (dashed), 100 and 1,000 throws  ·  1/6

Bayes · subjective probability
A probability is how sure you are, and evidence sharpens it.

The same throws, arriving one at a time. You never wait for the long run — early on you simply have a wider answer. Which is the only kind left when a thing happens once.

→ P( hypothesis | data ) — prior × likelihood

Whatever stands to the right of the bar is assumed. Whatever stands to the left is what the number is about. Both are probabilities — of different things.

Neyman-Pearson School Statistical Test

  • Frequentism
  • Null hypothesis vs. alternative hypothesis
    • Logic: if we reject the null hypothesis, we could support the alternative hypothesis, but we do not prove it
    • p-value: the probability of observing data as extreme as, or more extreme than, the actual observed data, given that the null hypothesis is true
Frequentist testing never tells you the probability that a hypothesis is true. It tells you how surprising your data would be if it were.

Achtung!!

  • The p-value is
    • NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true,
    • BUT the probability of observing data as extreme as, or more extreme than, the actual observed data, assuming the null hypothesis is true
This is the sentence most often got wrong in a thesis. Read it twice.

Neyman-Pearson school statistical test

  • Obtaining a p-value less than 0.05 provides evidence to reject the null hypothesis at the 5% significance level, but it does not mean we must reject it

  • Rejecting the null hypothesis suggests strong evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis, but it doesn’t definitively mean the alternative hypothesis is true

  • The test provides evidence against the null hypothesis but does not mean the alternative hypothesis is true, nor does it mean we can fully accept the alternative hypothesis

  • Hypothesis testing only indicates evidence, not a conclusive acceptance of any hypothesis

Neyman-Pearson school statistical test

  • Even if p-value is very low,
    • it DOES NOT mean that the alternative hypothesis is necessarily true
  • Even if p-value is very high,
    • it DOES NOT mean that the null hypothesis is necessarily true
A p-value is evidence, not a verdict. The 0.05 is a convention, and you are allowed to say so.

Neyman-Pearson school statistical test

What happens if the null hypothesis cannot be rejected?

  • It DOES NOT mean that the null hypothesis is necessarily true
  • In statistical testing, we never claim that
    1. the null hypothesis is true or
    2. the alternative hypothesis is true
  • We can only decide to reject or not reject the null hypothesis

If you're not comfortable with this sort of reasoning, you might consider using Bayesian statistics or a machine learning approach...

Neyman-Pearson school statistical test

  • When you select genes with a p-value below 0.05

you are choosing genes

  • that show evidence of differential expression at a significance level where the false positive rate is 5%, under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true (= the genes are not differentially expressed).

but normally practically we say, they are differentially expressed genes...

→\rightarrow What is the FPR (False Positive Rate)?

Statistical hypothesis test

  • V: False positive, Type I error
  • S: True positive
  • T: False negative, Type II error
  • U: True negative
Four boxes. Every error rate in this lecture is a ratio of two of them — the difficulty is that you can only ever count the column, never the row.

FPR, FDR

  • FPR = FP/(FP+TN) = V/(V+U)
  • FDR = FP/(FP+TP) = V/(V+S)

FPR: False Positive Rate

FDR: False Discovery Rate

FPR divides by the genes that are truly unchanged. FDR divides by the genes you actually called. Only the second denominator is something you can count.

Hypotheses Example

  • Null hypothesis
    H0H_{0}: the gene is not differentially expressed
  • Alternative hypothsis
    H1H_{1}: the gene is differentially expressed
The null hypothesis is one gene at a time — and Wednesday's practical tests it about ten thousand times in one run. That number is the whole problem.

FPR, FDR Example

Same table, two questions. Which denominator you use decides which one you are answering.

FPR, FDR Example

p-value & FDR

Example

  • p-value < 0.05
  • FDR < 0.05

What is the difference?

p-value & FDR

  • p-value < 0.05

    5% of the time, we may incorrectly reject the null hypothesis (i.e., incorrectly detect non-DEGs as DEGs)
    e.g. In a dataset of 10,000 non-DEGs, this could lead to approximately 500 non-DEGs being falsely identified as DEGs.

Five per cent of 10,000 unchanged genes is 500 false calls — before a single real one.

p-value & FDR

  • FDR < 0.05

    Among the genes detected as differentially expressed (DEGs), we expect that approximately 5% are false positives (non-DEGs).
    e.g., if 500 DEGs are detected, an FDR < 0.05 would suggest that around 25 of these could be non-DEGs (false positives).

FDR does not promise you no false positives. It promises you a known proportion of them among your calls.

Multiple testing problem

Wikipedia

In statistics, the multiple comparisons, multiplicity
or multiple testing problem occurs when one considers
a set of statistical inferences simultaneously.

Errors in inference, including confidence intervals
that fail to include their corresponding population
parameters or hypothesis tests that incorrectly reject
the null hypothesis are more likely to occur when
one considers the set as a whole.

Multiple testing problem

  • If you do a statistical test 3 times with p-value < 0.05
  • the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis becomes at least once

1−(1−0.05)×(1−0.05)×(1−0.05)≈0.1431-(1-0.05) \times (1-0.05) \times (1-0.05) \approx 0.143

→\rightarrow14.3% familywise error rate

Three tests, and the chance of at least one false alarm is already 14 %. Now imagine thirty-three thousand.

Familywise error rate Example

The error rate you control per test is not the error rate you get across a family of tests.

Example 100,000 times T-test

  • 2 sets of 20 normal random numbers
  • T-test 10,000 times
  • p-value distribution
Nothing is differentially expressed here — the data is random numbers. Whatever comes out is the false positive rate made visible.

Example 100,000 times T-test

R

p_value <- c()
    for(i in 1:100000){
        x1 <- rnorm(20)
        x2 <- rnorm(20)
        pv <- t.test(x1, x2)$p.value
        p_value <- c(p_value, pv)
    }
hist(p_value)

Example 100,000 times T-test

How many false positives if you reject the null hypotheses with significance level 5%?

Example 100,000 times T-test

FPR = 5%, #False Positives = 100,000 * 0.05 = 5,000, in case that you reject null hypotheses with significance level 5%

e.g. 5,000 genes might be detected for differentially expressed genes in 100,000 genes, even if they were not differentially expressed

Five thousand significant results out of pure noise. Anyone reporting a gene list without correction is showing you this histogram.

Correction p-value

Correction familywise error rate

  • Bonferroni method:
    • simple, very conservative

Calculate FDR from p-values

  • Benjamini-Hochberg method
    • simple, popular
Benjamini Y. Hochberg, et al., 1995
Bonferroni controls the chance of any false positive. BH controls the fraction of them among your calls. On ten thousand genes the first is so strict that almost nothing survives it.

Correction p-value

Correction familywise error rate

  • Bonferroni method
    simple, very conservative
    significant level α / the number of tests N

R

q.values <- p.adjust(p.values, method = "bonferroni")
Dividing 0.05 by ten thousand gives a threshold of 5 × 10−6. Correct, and in a course-sized experiment, useless.

Correction p-value

Calculate FDR from p-values

  • Benjamini-Hochberg method
    simple, popular

R

q.values <- p.adjust(p.values, method = "BH")
Benjamini Y. Hochberg, et al., 1995
This is the one you will use. p.adjust(p, method = "BH"), and edgeR's FDR column is exactly this.

Benjamini-Hochberg method

Algorithm

1.Sort p-values: p1≤p2≤p3≤…≤pNp_1 \leq p_{2} \leq p_{3} \leq \dots \leq p_{N}

2.Calculate: qm=pmN/m,m=1,…,Nq_m = p_m N / m, m=1,\dots,N

3.If qi>qjq_i > q_j then qi=qj,i,j=1,…,N,i<jq_i=q_j, i,j=1,…,N, i<j

Y. Benjamini, Y. Hochberg, 1995
Sort, scale by rank, then enforce monotonicity. Three lines of arithmetic, and the reason gene lists are publishable at all.

Exercise: Benjamini-Hochberg by hand

Five genes, already sorted by p-value. N = 5

m gene p
1 GeneA 0.002
2 GeneB 0.013
3 GeneC 0.039
4 GeneD 0.041
5 GeneE 0.600

Apply the three steps, then count the genes you would call at

  1. p < 0.05
  2. FDR < 0.05 (Benjamini-Hochberg)
  3. Bonferroni, significance level 0.05
Multiply by N/m. No calculator — and step 3 of the algorithm does something here.

Benjamini-Hochberg method 100,000 times T-test

Mostly ~ 1.0, null hypotheses cannot be rejected

The same random data, corrected: nothing survives. That is the right answer, and it is a result.

T-test

Problems

  • Each gene's spread is measured from its own three numbers
    • a coarse ruler, and no gene helps another
  • Counts are not normal — the spread grows with the mean
Student built the t-test for three samples, so three is not the objection. Measuring each gene alone is — and that is the one thing edgeR does differently.

Fisher's exact test

Problem

  • There is no consideration of biological replicates variation
Fisher's exact test compares two pooled counts — it cannot see that your three replicates disagreed with each other.

Likelihood ratio test LRT

  • Null model: no DEGs
  • Alternative model: DEGs
  • Deviance follows χ^2 distribution and calculate p-value
Fit two models, compare how well each explains the counts, and turn the difference into a p-value. That is what edgeR does per gene.

What is likelihood?

A likelihood function (often simply the likelihood)
is a function of the parameters of a statistical model
given data.(Wikipedia)
  • Mathematically equal to joint probability
  • How much probable the model fits to the data with the parameter(s)
Probability asks: given the model, how likely is this data? Likelihood asks the same question backwards: given this data, how good is the model?

Example Likelihood

Supposing that

  • You got 10 samples from a normal distributed population
    x=(x1,x2,…,x10)x=(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{10})
  • You do not know the mean and variance of the distribution

figures come from: https://www.kobiwa.jp/2019/12/03/post-777/ (Japanese)

Same ten numbers throughout. All that changes is the parameters we try.

Example likelihood

Normal distribution probability density function

Likelihood function

The likelihood of the whole sample is the product over the samples — which is why it is always computed as a sum of logs.

Likelihood = -568.93...

A poor guess at the parameters. Remember the number.

Likelihood = -20.04... got bigger

figures come from: https://www.kobiwa.jp/2019/12/03/post-777/ (Japanese)

A better guess, and the likelihood rises. Fitting a model means searching for the guess that makes it highest.

Mini summary

  • Joint probability

    • assumption: given a distribution function
    • input: samples
    • output: probability

  • Likelihood

    • assumption: given samples
    • input: parameters of distribution function
    • output: likelihood

Likelihood ratio test

  • 2 models distribution function
    1. estimate parameters using genei_i expressions in both A and B group
    2. estimate parameters using genei_i expressions in A and B group, independently
  • calculate
    1. likelihood ratio
    2. Deviance
    3. p-value, FDR
Model 1 says both groups share one mean; model 2 lets them differ. The ratio of the two likelihoods is the evidence that they do.

Likelihood ratio test / Example cheat coin toss

Imagine a cheating coin toss...

Likelihood ratio test / Example cheat coin toss

Coin toss 10 times each

  • Person A: heads 5, tails 5
  • Person B: heads 9, tails 1

→\longrightarrow Are they using certainly the same coin?

Ten tosses each. Your intuition already says B is cheating — the test is how to say it with a number.

Likelihood ratio test / Example cheat coin toss

Parameter (of distribution function): the probability of heads H

null model:

L(H0)=0.55×0.55×0.59×0.51=9.54×10−7L(H0) = 0.5^5 × 0.5^5 × 0.5^9 × 0.5^1 = 9.54 × 10^{-7}

alternative model:

L(H1)=0.55×0.55×0.99×0.11=3.78×10−5L(H1) = 0.5^5 × 0.5^5 × 0.9^9 × 0.1^1 = 3.78 × 10^{-5}

Under the null both coins are fair. Under the alternative each has its own bias. Two parameters instead of one.

Likelihood ratio test LRT

  • Null model: no DEGs
  • Alternative model: DEGs
  • Deviance follows χ^2 distribution and calculate p-value

Likelihood ratio test Example cheat coin toss

Likelihood

L(H0)=0.520=9.53×10−7L(H0) = 0.5^{20} = 9.53 × 10^{-7} L(H1)=0.55×0.55×0.99×0.11=3.78×10−5L(H1) = 0.5^5 × 0.5^5 × 0.9^9 × 0.1^1 = 3.78 × 10^{-5}

Likelihood ratio

  • λ=L(H0)/L(H1)=9.54×10−7/3.78×10−5=0.025\lambda = L(H0)/L(H1) = 9.54 × 10^{-7} / 3.78 \times 10^{-5} = 0.025
  • D=−2log(λ)=−2log(0.025)D = -2log(\lambda) = -2log(0.025) =7.36= 7.36

D (Deviance) becomes low if the two coins are same...

p-value

> pchisq(7.36, df=1, lower.tail=FALSE)
[1] 0.00667
D = 7.36 on one degree of freedom gives p = 0.0067. The single degree of freedom is the one extra parameter the alternative model was allowed.

Functional analysis

Goal: Understand the biological meaning of differentially expressed genes (DEGs)

  • Gene Ontology analysis

    • Biological process, Molecular function, Cellular component

  • Pathway analysis

    • KEGG, Reactome, MSigDB, etc.
A list of gene identifiers is not a result. Functional analysis is the step where it becomes one.

Gene Ontology

Structured controlled vocabularies ontologies that describe gene products in terms of their associated

  1. Biological Processes (BP)
  2. Cellular Components (CC)
  3. Molecular Functions (MF)

http://www.geneontology.org/GO.doc.shtml

A controlled vocabulary is the point: two labs annotating the same gene must use the same words, or nothing can be compared.

Ontology structure

  • Acyclic Graph Tree Structure
  • Node: GO term
A term has more than one parent, so GO is a graph and not a tree. That is why a gene counted under one term is also counted under its ancestors.

GO term, GO ID

Example

  • ATCG00080.1 (photosystem II reaction center protein I)
    • GO:0015979 : photosynthesis (BP)
    • GO:0016020 : membrane (CC)
One gene, several terms, in several ontologies at once. There is no single 'function' column.

Exercise

Example

  • ATCG00080.1 (photosystem II reaction center protein I)

Search

  • http://www.arabidopsis.org/

GO Relations

  1. is a
  2. part of
  3. regulates
Three relations, and only the first two are inherited upwards in the way you expect.

'is a', 'part of'

mitochondrion has two parents: it is an organelle and it is part of the cytoplasm

organelle has two children: mitochondrion is an organelle, and organelle membrane is part of organelle

Annotate a gene to a child term and it is annotated to every ancestor as well. Enrichment tests depend on this.

'regulates'

regulation of mitotic spindle organization regulates mitotic spindle organization and mitotic spindle organization is part of the mitotic cell cycle

therefore regulation of mitotic spindle organization regulates the mitotic cell cycle

regulates crosses between branches, which is exactly why the graph is not a tree.

Practice

Functional analysis/Enrichment analysis


Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) is a method to identify classes of genes or proteins that are over- represented in a large set of genes or proteins (Wikipedia)

Aravind Subramanian, et al., PNAS, 102 (43), 15545--15550, 2005.

Enrichment asks whether your gene list contains more of a category than chance would give. Everything below is a way of making 'more than chance' precise.

ORA vs GSEA: Two approaches to functional analysis

Over-Representation Analysis (ORA)

  • Uses a selected gene list (e.g., DEGs with FDR < 0.05)
  • Tests if functional categories are enriched in the selected genes
  • Simple and intuitive

Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)

  • Uses all genes ranked by expression change
  • Tests if functional categories are enriched at extremes of the ranking
  • More sensitive to small but coordinated changes

ORA: Step-by-Step Process

  1. Select DEGs (e.g., FDR < 0.05)
  2. For each GO term, build the contingency table below
  3. Fisher's exact test: Is 'a' larger than expected by chance?
  4. Multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg)
DEGsnon-DEGs
In GO termab
Not in termcd
ORA throws away the ranking and keeps only the membership. Simple, and it depends entirely on where you put the FDR cut.

Example, Fisher's exact test

DEGs non DEGs
GOID:0001 10 100
Other than GOID:0001 100 1000 
> fisher.test(matrix(c(10,100,100,1000), nrow=2))

    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  matrix(c(10, 100, 100, 1000), nrow = 2)
p-value = 1
10 of 110 in the term against 100 of 1,100 outside: the same proportion, and no enrichment.

Example, Fisher's exact test

DEGs non DEGs
GOID:0001 25 100
Other than GOID:0001 100 1000 
> fisher.test(matrix(c(25,100,100,1000), nrow=2))

    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  matrix(c(25, 100, 100, 1000), nrow = 2)
p-value = 0.0004687
Raise 10 to 25 and nothing else, and it becomes significant. The test is doing arithmetic on the ratio, not on the biology.

GSEA: The ranking approach

  1. Rank all genes by expression change (e.g., logFC, t-statistic)
  2. For each gene set, calculate enrichment score (ES)
  3. ES: How much are gene set members enriched at extremes?
  4. Permutation test: Generate null distribution of ES
  5. Calculate p-value and FDR

No arbitrary cutoff needed!

GSEA never draws a line. It uses every gene and asks where in the ranking a category piles up.

GSEA: Enrichment score calculation

The Walking Statistic:

  • Start from top of ranked gene list
  • For each gene:
    • If in gene set: ES goes up
    • If not in set: ES goes down
  • Maximum deviation from zero = Enrichment Score

Positive ES: Gene set enriched at top (up-regulated)
Negative ES: Gene set enriched at bottom (down-regulated)

Walk down the ranked list, up for a hit and down for a miss. The furthest the walk gets from zero is the score.

GSEA: Simple example - setup

Setting: 7 genes ranked by logFC, 3 genes in "metabolism" gene set

Walking Score Calculation Rules

  • Hit a metabolism gene: +1
  • Hit an other gene: -1
  • Cumulative calculation
  • Enrichment Score (ES) = maximum deviation from zero

Case 1 - Metabolism genes enriched at top

Rank  Gene   logFC  Gene set      Score  Walking score
1     GeneA   2.5   Metabolism     +1      +1
2     GeneB   2.0   Metabolism     +1      +2  
3     GeneC   1.8   Metabolism     +1      +3   ← ES = +3
4     GeneD   1.2   Other          -1      +2
5     GeneE   0.8   Other          -1      +1
6     GeneF   0.3   Other          -1       0
7     GeneG  -0.2   Other          -1      -1

ES = +3 (positive → metabolism genes up-regulated)

Case 2 - Metabolism genes randomly distributed

Rank  Gene   logFC  Gene set      Score  Walking score  
1     GeneA   2.5   Metabolism     +1      +1   ← ES = +1
2     GeneB   2.0   Other          -1       0
3     GeneC   1.8   Other          -1      -1
4     GeneD   1.2   Metabolism     +1       0
5     GeneE   0.8   Other          -1      -1
6     GeneF   0.3   Metabolism     +1       0
7     GeneG  -0.2   Other          -1      -1

ES = +1 (small positive → weak enrichment)

Interpretation: Case 1 shows clear up-regulation of metabolism genes, while Case 2 shows random distribution.

GSEA p-value calculation - step 1

Calculate actual ES from real data

Real data:
Rank  Gene   logFC  Gene set      Walking score
1     GeneA   2.5   Metabolism     +1
2     GeneB   2.0   Metabolism     +2  
3     GeneC   1.8   Metabolism     +3   ← Actual ES = +3
4     GeneD   1.2   Other          +2
5     GeneE   0.8   Other          +1
6     GeneF   0.3   Other           0
7     GeneG  -0.2   Other          -1

Actual ES = +3

GSEA p-value calculation - step 2

Generate null distribution by permutation

Permutation: Randomly shuffle gene set labels (keep ranking unchanged)

Permutation 1:
Rank  Gene   logFC  Shuffled set   Walking score
1     GeneA   2.5   Other          -1
2     GeneB   2.0   Metabolism     +0  ← ES = +0
3     GeneC   1.8   Other          -1
...

Permutation 2:
1     GeneA   2.5   Metabolism     +1  ← ES = +1
2     GeneB   2.0   Other           0
3     GeneC   1.8   Metabolism     +1
...

Repeat 1000+ times → Get 1000+ null ES values

GSEA p-value calculation - step 3

Compare actual ES with null distribution

Null ES distribution from permutations:
     Frequency
        |     /\
        |    /  \
        |   /    \
        |__/______\______ ES value
        -2  -1  0  1  2  3
                      ↑
                 Actual ES = +3

p-value = (Number of permutation ES ≥ +3) / (Total permutations)

Example: If only 5 out of 1000 permutations gave ES ≥ +3 → p-value = 5/1000 = 0.005

Interpretation: Only 0.5% chance to get ES ≥ +3 by random chance → Statistically significant enrichment

ORA vs GSEA: key differences

ORA (Over-Representation Analysis)

  • Input: DEG list (e.g., genes with FDR < 0.05)
  • Question: "Is this GO term significantly enriched in DEGs?"
  • Statistical method: Fisher's exact test

GSEA (Gene Set Enrichment Analysis)

  • Input: All genes ranked by logFC
  • Question: "Are genes in this GO term enriched at the top/bottom of the ranking?"
  • Statistical method: Kolmogorov-Smirnov-like test

When to use which?

  • Clear DEG list available → ORA
  • Want to capture subtle changes → GSEA
  • In practice, often use both methods

Functional Analysis

  • Enrichment analysis reveals biological meaning of DEGs
  • Identifies over-represented GO categories and pathways
  • Two main approaches: ORA (selected gene lists) and GSEA (ranked gene lists)

All of these want a gene list, so all of them inherit whatever threshold you chose. Say which threshold in the report.

R packages Bioconductor

  • topGO https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/topGO.html
  • goseq http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/goseq.html
  • GOstats https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/GOstats.html
  • clusterProfiler https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/clusterProfiler.html
topGO is the one on fgcz-kl-004, and the one the DEG practical uses. It needs the gene-to-GO table you are asked to reconstruct.
